title: Maybe We Don't Need the Store: How Living Goods Began in Uganda
dek: After pushing Kenyan shop clerks out to sell in schools and churches, Chuck Slaughter dropped the shop altogether and, with BRAC, sent women door to door in Uganda.

story.event: Dropping the shop for door-to-door health promoters and piloting the model in Uganda with BRAC
story.summary: After selling TravelSmith in 2004, Chuck Slaughter worked on turning around Kenya's struggling Child and Family Wellness drug shops and found sales came when clerks went out to schools and churches. He studied Avon as a sales representative, founded the nonprofit Living Goods and in 2007 began piloting door-to-door women health promoters in Uganda with BRAC. A randomised trial in 214 Ugandan villages later found under-five mortality about 27 per cent lower where promoters worked.
paragraphs: In 2004 Chuck Slaughter sold TravelSmith, the mail-order travel clothing company he had built, and took on a very different job: turning around the Child and Family Wellness Shops, a struggling chain of small franchised drug shops in Kenya. What finally worked, he told the Stanford Social Innovation Review in 2008, was getting the clerks "off their tails" and sending them out of the shops to sell in schools and churches.

It set him thinking: "maybe we don't need the store at all. Maybe it's not McDonald's we want to imitate, but Avon." To learn how Avon worked, he signed up as a sales representative. "While I can't say I knocked the lights out of lipstick sales, I did learn quite a bit," he told NBC News in 2013. He was surprised to find the company had begun in rural America in the 19th century, and saw a parallel with remote African villages, where shops were hard to reach and medicine was often overpriced, out of stock or fake.

Rather than open more shops, he set up a nonprofit, Living Goods, and in 2007 it began piloting the idea in Uganda with BRAC, the microfinance organisation. Women were chosen from among BRAC's existing borrowers. Each received a free starter kit of a uniform, a lockable storage chest and a banner, and a below-market BRAC loan to buy stock from Living Goods, and kept the margin on what she sold: malaria and diarrhoea treatments, bed nets, water treatment and soap, priced below the local shops. Each needed at least 150 households within walking or cycling distance, and first visited every home on her map to take a health survey. By autumn 2008, promoters were working in 200 Ugandan communities.

Whether a sales margin would save lives, and not just sell soap, was still untested. Economists ran a randomised trial across 214 villages from 2011 to 2013, and reported in 2019 that where promoters worked, deaths of children under five were about 27 per cent lower, at roughly $68 per life-year saved. By the end of 2013 the programme reached 883 villages, and by the end of 2018 more than 7,000. The pay stayed modest: NPR reported in 2016 that an average agent earned $10 to $20 a month.

quote.text: Yet, the right act Is less, far less, than the right-thinking mind. Seek refuge in thy soul; have there thy heaven! Scorn them that follow virtue for her gifts!
quote.locator: Chapter II, "Sankhya-Yog, or The Book of Doctrines" (verse 49 in the Sanskrit numbering)
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: Slaughter built Living Goods on the bet that a margin on soap and malaria pills would keep health workers knocking on doors. The Gita scorns those who follow virtue for her gifts. The trial found that unpaid services rose too, which suggests mixed motives; it cannot say which one saved the children.

reflection: Living Goods never asked its promoters to choose between earning and caring. It built the earning in on purpose, because goodwill alone had a habit of running out. The Gita asks something harder: whether the work would still be right if nothing came back from it.

You do not have to settle that this morning. Most of what you do mixes the two, as theirs did, and mixed motives are not a failing. It can still help to know which parts of your week you would keep doing for nothing, because those parts tend to hold up in the weeks when the rest does not.
invitation: Name one task this week you would do even if it paid nothing, and one you do mainly because it pays. Write both down without judging either, then get on with the day.

cross_checks.claim: After selling TravelSmith in 2004, Slaughter worked on turning around a struggling nonprofit drug-shop franchise in Kenya (the Child and Family Wellness Shops).
Slaughter signed up as an Avon sales representative to study the direct-selling model before building Living Goods on it.
Living Goods began its door-to-door health promoter work in Uganda with BRAC in 2007.
Promoters bought products at wholesale and earned a margin on what they sold, rather than working as volunteers or salaried staff.
A randomised trial found under-five mortality about 27 per cent lower where promoters worked, at about $68 per life-year saved.

research_notes: Founding year: NPR (2016) says Slaughter founded Living Goods in 2006; NBC (2013) and GOOD (2011) say 2007; SSIR's Fall 2008 piece says the nonprofit was founded the year before; GOOD says the first branch opened in 2008; the AEJ paper says Living Goods and BRAC Uganda began piloting the model in 2007 (its cost table separately dates Living Goods' own Uganda operations from 2010, presumably its directly run branches). The story therefore does not give a founding year and dates only the BRAC pilot to 2007. Kenya role: SSIR says he was 'hired' in 2004 to turn around the Child and Family Wellness Shops; Entrepreneur says he 'volunteered to help run' a nonprofit drugstore franchise; the story says he 'took on' the job and does not say whether he was paid. Prices: SSIR cites oral rehydration salts at 30 per cent below market, Entrepreneur 20 to 40 per cent below, GOOD up to 40 per cent, and the AEJ paper a target of about 10 per cent below for health products; the story says only 'below the local shops'. Reach figures disagree across sources and dates and were not used beyond the dated ones: CSMonitor (2013) says 975 representatives treated more than 200,000 children in 2012, while Entrepreneur (2014) gives 62,000 children treated in 2013; agent counts run from 200 communities (2008) to about 650 agents (2011), 975 (2012), over 1,000 (2014) and about 4,000 (NPR 2016). The story uses SSIR's 2008 community count and the AEJ village counts. Recruitment: SSIR (2008) describes agents drawn from BRAC's borrowers; the AEJ paper describes a later competitive selection of women aged 18 to 45 with two weeks' training; the story describes only the early pilot. Earnings of $10 to $20 a month are NPR's figure, attributed to NPR. The trial result (27 per cent, $68 per life-year) is the authors' published estimate; BRAC's page gives the same figures. The AEJ paper is cited from IPA's hosted PDF; it loads but the checker cannot read its text, so the trial is cross-checked against BRAC's summary. The Gita line is Arnold's verse rendering within Chapter II; the Sanskrit verse number is given only as a guide, since Arnold does not number verses.
